title: The Fee You Never Repriced: What Rising Payment Costs Are Quietly Taking Off Every Sale
linkedin:
Your Christmas trading revenue is about to climb. So is the average cost of simply getting paid.

Most owner-led businesses set their card surcharge or signed up for a buy now pay later provider years ago, priced it in once, and never looked at it again since. Acceptance costs have crept up, and the share of sales running through the more expensive payment methods has quietly grown.

Here is the pattern we see most often across owner-led businesses heading into their busiest quarter: revenue rises and the cost of collecting it rises too, but because both move gradually, neither shows up as one alarming number on the P&L. It shows up later, as a margin that stops tracking the sales line the way it used to.

Buy now pay later is often priced at a multiple of what a standard card transaction costs the business, not the customer. A business that let its buy now pay later share grow from a sliver of sales to a third of them has effectively repriced itself downward without a single conversation about it.

The fix is not banning convenient payment methods. It is pulling twelve months of settlement reports by payment type, working out the true blended cost of acceptance, and comparing it to whatever rate was last used to set prices or surcharges. Then deciding, on purpose, whether to pass it through, build it into the price, or absorb it with full visibility.

That is the kind of line by line review worth doing before the Christmas volume hits, not after.

Spring is the time most Queensland and East Coast business owners are locking in Christmas stock, casual staff and marketing spend for the final quarter of the year. While you are planning for the revenue lift, it is worth checking one thing that rarely gets a second look: what it actually costs you to get paid.

Card surcharges, tap and go fees and buy now pay later providers like Afterpay and Zip all cost different amounts, and most businesses set these up once and never revisit them. Over time those costs tend to creep up, and the share of sales running through the more expensive payment methods tends to grow too, especially during the gift buying months.

The result is a pattern we see often: revenue goes up heading into the busy season, and the cost of collecting that revenue goes up right alongside it. Because both move gradually, it rarely looks like a problem on paper. It shows up later as a margin that does not track sales the way it used to.

The fix is not complicated. Pull your settlement reports, work out your true blended cost of accepting payment, and compare it to whatever rate you last used to set your prices or surcharges. Worth doing before the Christmas volume hits rather than after.
